title: What Is an Agent, Really?
transcript: You've been using agents for years. You just didn't know it. The filter that moves a newsletter out of your inbox. The phone that says traffic is heavy, leave now. The playlist that somehow knows your taste. Each one watches something, decides something, and acts.
The agents in this guide are the same idea, only much bigger. They don't do one clever thing. They do many things in a row, adapting as they go.

Every agent runs the same loop. Observe: take in what's there. Plan: decide what to do. Act: do it. Check: did it work? If not, round it goes again, with what it just learned. A simple agent goes round once. A powerful one goes round dozens of times.

What an agent can do depends on its tools. Picture a smart new employee at an empty desk. Clever, but stuck. Give them a login, and they can track the work. A key to the project, and they can change it. A key to launch, and they can ship it. The tools are the access, and you decide which keys to hand over.

An agent is not a person. It has no goals and no feelings. It predicts the most useful next step from what it can see. So you don't need to motivate it. You need to be clear. And it will be confidently wrong. It will solve the wrong problem with beautiful precision, and keep going, tirelessly, in the wrong direction.

Agents come in a spectrum. Autocomplete guesses your next word. Chat assistants answer your questions. Tool-equipped agents have hands: they read files and run commands. And autonomous agents work on their own for long stretches. You can close your laptop, and come back to finished work, waiting for your review.

One more idea. The model is the engine. The program around it, the harness, is the car. Every approval prompt you've ever clicked came from the harness. So when an agent does something reckless, ask two questions. Why did it suggest that? And why was it allowed? The second one is a setting. And settings are yours.

So your job isn't typing. It's steering. Agents work in a loop. Tools set what they can do. Check their work, and be clear. If you've ever managed people, you already have the core skill. Next up: How to Give Good Instructions.

title: How to Give Good Instructions
transcript: Two people want the same thing: a simple dashboard of their team's weekly sales. Alex types five words. Make me a sales dashboard. The agent builds something with charts. But the numbers are fake. It shows months, not weeks. It uses a chart library Alex has never heard of. Two hours of fixes later, Alex gives up.

Maya opens the same agent and writes a few clear lines. Connect to our real sales data. Show the last eight weeks as a stacked bar chart, one colour per person. Use the chart library we already have. Match our blue header and white cards. The agent builds exactly that. First try. Same agent, same goal. The only difference was the instructions.

A good instruction has three parts. What you want, said specifically, because when an agent guesses, it guesses confidently. Why it matters, so it understands the problem, not just the feature. And how you'll know it worked. That's the part most people skip, and it's the one that lets the agent check its own work.

Then say what not to do. Agents are eager. Ask one to fix a button colour, and it might redesign the whole screen. Constraints are lane markers on a road. Don't change the existing pages. Don't add new tools. Use the colours we already have. Inside the lanes, the agent drives freely. It just can't cross the lines.

Instructions come in levels. Level zero is a wish: make the app better. Level one is a goal: add a way to export data. Level two is a specification: an export button on the settings page, with these columns and this file name. Level three is a full blueprint, usually more than you need. For most tasks, level two is the sweet spot.

And before anything gets built, ask for a plan. Don't change anything yet. Tell me what you'll build, and how you'll check it. Then read that plan the way you'd read a builder's quote for a kitchen. It's the cheapest review you'll ever do. A wrong assumption in a ten line plan costs one sentence to fix. Found after the build, it costs an afternoon.

When something is still off, don't just say: that's not right, fix it. That's Captain Alex again. Be targeted. The chart shows monthly totals; change it to weekly. What's wrong, what you want instead, and how to check it.
An agent is only as good as the job you describe. How you explain the job matters more than the tool doing it. Next up: context in, verification out.
